comments.text: It was heavily discussed a few years ago, for example in [LINK] They last for a log time, but the important detail is that they have very low power, like 1mW with the size factor of a normal battery, so you need like a dozen for a (old) wrist watch and s few hundred to turn on a led. comments.author: mikewarot
comments.story: Ask HN: What under-the-radar technology are you excited about?
comments.text: Why are you interested in this? If it is for anything other than very LOW power (microwatts), you're going to be disappointed. It is essentially a beta emitter hooked to a capacitor via some electronics to handle voltage conversion. The thing is the beta source is use it or lose it, and very low power. If you scaled this up to power a Tesla, it would be a nightmare, as it would need to dissipate the full power the car requires, all the time, or it would melt down (aka Fukashima) For a longer debunk - [VIDEO]

comments.story: Nano-diamond battery that "lasts for 28k years" closer to commercialization
comments.text: EEVblog did a debunk of this at [VIDEO] Basically, the power density of these are so low that they're useless for most applications. Sure, it might last 28,000 years, but you're only getting 100 microwatts from a battery the size of a normal AA battery.
